What have you got going on that trumps being there when your dad passes? Most other things can wait a little. Particularly if he's still in possession of his mind and memory.

Sit with him and talk about the things you might like to do after he passes, as a kind of trade off for delaying doing what he's asking you. Places you might like to travel. See if he has any suggestions for places to visit. Maybe do something like buy a bag of colored stones, set them out and ask him where he wants you place each one around the country. So when you travel you have a little task you can perform for him, like he was there with you. He may have very specific places he remembers from his past that he might like to show you by proxy. Or even a time-based release plan, of placing one at a certain place at a certain time, or throwing one into a certain pond or lake or body of water some NYE, Christmas, Birthday or other meaningful date.

Don't rush him. Let him think and ponder over it. Get his mind out and away from his body and present condition. If he had the ability and health, where would he want to place these stones to mark some special memory before he died.

Tell him how you feel. Odds are he's got some sort of pride/guilt/hero complex thing going on.

If you remind him how much you love spending time with him and that you'll have plenty of time when he's gone to do other things, he'll probably get over it.

Is your dad getting all the help he needs? Are all of his spiritual, financial, social, and medical needs being met as much as possible? Is he comfortable? You don't mention if he is at home or in a care facility. You don't mention if he is alone or if he has friends and family around him. If he has everyone else, then maybe he sees how uncomfortable you are, and is giving you permission to step away. If you are his only or chief support, then you must stay to be his advocate and his voice to get additional help. Even if he is in a care facility, he needs someone to speak up for him, and ensure he is getting the best care possible. It matters.
